IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020
SUHAS CHAKMA                      ….PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA AND
OTHERS                      ….RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 182 OF 2025
O R D E R
1. This  Court  having  considered  the  various
issues  arising  in  relation  to  the  functioning,
governance and management of Open Correctional
Institutions1 (“OCIs”), and having also taken into
consideration the reports submitted by the learned
1  For short, “OCIs”.
1

--- Page 55 ---
Amicus  Curiae  in this regard,  vide its judgment
dated 26 th February, 2026 in  Suhas Chakma v.
Union of India 2, proceeded to issue exhaustive
directions with a view to giving meaningful effect to
the  reformative  and  rehabilitative  objectives
underlying the establishment of OCIs, including
directions  concerning  their  effective  functioning,
uniformity in standards, expansion of infrastructure
and  continued  monitoring  and  compliance.  In
particular, noticing the absence of uniformity in the
governance, eligibility norms, rehabilitative facilities
and management of OCIs across the States and
Union  Territories,  this  Court,  directed  the
constitution of a  High-Powered  Committee  for
Reform  and  Governance  of  Open  Correctional
Institutions3, with Hon’ble Mr. Justice S. Ravindra
Bhat, Judge (Retd.), Supreme Court of India, as its
Executive Chairperson.
2. The High-Powered Committee was entrusted
with,  inter  alia , the task of formulating Common
Minimum  Standards  for  the  governance,
2  Writ Petition (Civil) No. 1082 of 2020.
3  Hereinafter, being referred to as “High-Powered 
Committee”.
2

--- Page 56 ---
administration  and  management  of  OCIs;
harmonising correctional practices across the States
and Union Territories; identifying systemic gaps in
the existing legal and administrative frameworks;
recommending standardized eligibility assessment
protocols; and formulating enforceable guidelines to
ensure  gender-sensitive,  inclusive  and  non-
discriminatory access to OCIs. The High-Powered
Committee  was  further  required  to  recommend
measures concerning capacity-building of prison
officials,  periodic  monitoring,  data  collection,
evaluation and audit of OCIs, as well as inter-
agency  coordination  amongst  the  concerned
authorities. This Court directed the High-Powered
Committee  to  submit  a  comprehensive  report
containing  its recommendations, along  with the
draft  Common  Minimum  Standards,  preferably
within six months from the date of its first meeting.
3. Subsequently, by judgment dated 21 st April,
2026 in  Sathyan Naravoor v. Union of India 4,
this Court directed the High-Powered Committee to
further examine compliance by all States and Union
4  Writ Petition (Civil) No. 182 of 2025.
3

--- Page 57 ---
Territories  with  the  directions  issued  in  L.
Muruganatham v. State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. 5,
concerning the rights of prisoners with disabilities.
The High-Powered Committee was also directed to
formulate an action plan for provision of appropriate
assistive devices, mobility aids and other necessary
support equipment to prisoners with disabilities,
tailored  to  their  specific  needs  and  functional
requirements. 
4. Pursuant to the aforesaid judgments, the High-
Powered Committee has submitted a Status Report
dated 31 st August, 2026, detailing out the steps
taken  by  it  towards  discharging  the  mandate
entrusted to it by this Court. The report, inter alia ,
records  the  constitution  of  the  High-Powered
Committee,  the  steps  taken  for  securing  the
requisite  nominations  and  participation  of  the
concerned authorities from the States and Union
Territories, and the convening of its meetings on 6 th
May, 2026 and 26 th May, 2026. The High-Powered
Committee has also undertaken the exercise of
collecting  comprehensive  information  from  the
5  (2025) 10 SCC 401.
4

--- Page 58 ---
States  and  Union  Territories  regarding  the
administration and governance of OCIs, including
their infrastructure, rehabilitative and reformative
programmes, applicable rules and regulations, and
the best practices being followed therein.
5. The  High-Powered  Committee  has,  in
furtherance of its mandate, also undertaken on-the-
ground visits and inspections of OCIs, including the
OCI at Devanahalli, Bengaluru; the Karnal Open Air
Jail in Haryana;  and  the  Cherlapally  Prisoners
Agricultural Colony in Telangana, with a view to
assessing the prevailing conditions, nature of work,
availability of vocational training and educational
facilities, wages, healthcare and other rehabilitative
measures. The report records, inter alia, the need for
greater  utilisation  of  OCI  facilities;  widening  of
eligibility criteria; strengthening of skill development
and educational facilities; rationalisation of wages;
and identification of measures for facilitating the
inclusion of women prisoners and prisoners with
disabilities. Detailed questionnaires have also been
prepared  and  circulated  to  the  concerned
stakeholders to obtain granular information on the
5

--- Page 59 ---
administration and governance of OCIs, and the
High-Powered Committee proposes to consider these
issues and make preliminary recommendations at
its meeting scheduled for 8th September, 2026.
6. When  the  matter  was  taken  up  for
consideration on 3 rd September, 2026, the learned
Amicus Curiae pointed out that, having regard to the
mandate entrusted to the High-Powered Committee
and the steps required to be undertaken by it,
certain  procedural  and  administrative  directions
would be necessary to facilitate its smooth and
effective functioning. The necessary directions are
contained in paragraph 47 of the Status Report
submitted by the High-Powered Committee and,
inter alia , relate to ensuring effective representation
of  the  Secretaries  of  the  Department of  Social
Justice and Empowerment/Department of Social
Welfare of all States and Union Territories, or their
nominees  not  below  the  rank  of  Additional
Secretary,  before  the  High-Powered  Committee;
filing of compliance affidavits by the concerned
States and Union Territories in respect of the rights
of  prisoners  with  disabilities,  in  terms  of  the
6

--- Page 60 ---
directions contained in the judgment dated 21 st
April, 2026 in  Sathyan Naravoor v. Union of
India; and nomination of an officer of the Ministry
of Home Affairs to attend to the administrative
requirements of the High-Powered Committee and
participate in its ongoing meetings.
7. The learned Amicus Curiae further pointed out
that the High-Powered Committee is scheduled to
consider, at its meeting to be held on 8 th September,
2026, various issues falling within its mandate,
including  widening  of  the  eligibility  criteria  for
transfer to OCIs, measures for optimum utilisation
of existing OCI capacity, increase in the scale of
wages payable to prisoners, skill development and
employability measures, and measures for inclusion
of women prisoners. It was submitted that the High-
Powered Committee proposes to make preliminary
recommendations on these aspects following the
said meeting. The learned Amicus Curiae , therefore,
submitted that the matter may be deferred beyond
two weeks, so that the recommendations of the
High-Powered Committee may be placed before this
Court for its consideration.
7

--- Page 61 ---
8. Having considered the Status Report dated 31st
August,  2026  submitted  by  the  High-Powered
Committee, as well as the submissions advanced by
the learned Amicus Curiae, we are of the considered
view that, at this stage, the following directions are
necessary to facilitate the effective and smooth
functioning of the High-Powered Committee and to
further  the  objectives  underlying  the  directions
issued by this Court:
A. The  States  of  Andhra  Pradesh,  Arunachal
Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana,
Himachal  Pradesh,  Jharkhand,  Karnataka,
Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Manipur,
Mizoram, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Odisha, Punjab,
Tamil  Nadu,  Telangana,  Tripura  and  West
Bengal, and the Union Territories of Andaman &
Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar
Haveli  and  Daman  &  Diu,  Delhi,  Ladakh,
Lakshadweep,  Jammu  &  Kashmir  and
Puducherry, shall ensure effective representation
through the Secretaries of the Department of
Social Justice and Empowerment/Department of
Social Welfare, as the case may be, or its nominee
8

--- Page 62 ---
not below the rank of Additional Secretary, before
the  High-Powered  Committee,  in  terms  of
Direction 7(B)  contained in the judgment dated
21st April, 2026 in Sathyan Naravoor v. Union
of India, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 182 of 2025.
Any instance of non-compliance will be viewed
seriously. 
B. The  States  of  Andhra  Pradesh,  Arunachal
Pradesh,  Assam,  Bihar,  Chhattisgarh,  Goa,
Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka,
Kerala,  Madhya  Pradesh,  Manipur,  Mizoram,
Nagaland, Rajasthan,  Tamil Nadu, Telangana,
Tripura, Uttarakhand and West Bengal, and the
Union Territories of Andaman & Nicobar Islands,
Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman &
Diu, Delhi, Jammu & Kashmir, Lakshadweep,
Ladakh and Puducherry, shall file the requisite
compliance affidavits before the High-Powered
Committee in respect of the rights of prisoners
with  disabilities,  in  terms  of  Direction  7(C)
contained in the judgment dated 21 st April, 2026
in Sathyan Naravoor v. Union of India , Writ
Petition (Civil) No. 182 of 2025 within two weeks. 
9

--- Page 63 ---
C. The Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of
India, shall nominate an officer not below the

Committee and to participate in the ongoing
meetings of the High-Powered Committee.
9. The Registry is directed to transmit a copy of
this order to the Chief Secretaries of the States of
Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar,

hereinabove. A copy of this order shall also be
transmitted to the Home Secretary, Ministry of

UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                    O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The present special leave petitions call in question the

--- Page 82 ---
2
correctness  of  the  order  dated  13.08.2024  and  08.04.2025
passed by the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur
in S.B. Criminal Revision Petition No.1097 of 2019 whereby the
learned Single Judge of the High Court, while recalling the
order dated 18.02.2020 passed by the High Court, directed the
petitioner-accused to surrender before the Trial Court or
prison authorities, District Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan, to serve
the sentence as passed by the learned Judicial Magistrate,
Chidawa, in Criminal Case No. 85/2016.
BRIEF FACTS:-
3. Krishna  Kumar/Krishan  Kumar-the  Complainant-Respondent
herein filed a complaint against the petitioner-accused in the
Court of Judicial Magistrate, Chidawa, District Jhunjhunu,
Rajasthan, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments
Act, 1881 (for short ‘the NI Act’)stating that the complainant
and the petitioner-accused were well acquainted with each
other  and  for  business  purposes,  the  petitioner-accused
received        Rs. 22,50,000/- (Rupees Twenty Two Lakhs,
Fifty Thousand) in cash from the Complainant on 10.02.2014.
Reciprocally, the petitioner-accused issued a Cheque bearing
No. 001034 dated 10.02.2014 drawn on Axis Bank Ltd., Pilani
Branch. On 03.05.2014, when the cheque was presented for
payment by the complainant, the same was returned by the Bank
on 05.05.2014 stating ‘insufficient funds’. On being informed
of such dishonour of cheque, the petitioner-accused assured
the complainant to present the cheque again to the Bank. On
07.05.2014, the complainant presented the said cheque again

--- Page 83 ---
3
but the cheque got dishnoured due to ‘insufficient funds’. The
complainant again deposited the said cheque on 09.05.2014 with
the Bank but the cheque met the same fate.
4. Aggrieved,  the  complainant  sent  a  legal  notice  to
petitioner-accused on 19.05.2014 but the petitioner-accused
did not return the said amount to the complainant but the same
was returned with the remark “the addressee was not found at
home and the family members refused to receive it”.
5. In such circumstances, the complainant was constrained to
file a complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act before the
Court of Judicial Magistrate, Chidawa, which was registered as
Criminal Case No. 85/2016.
6. The Court of Judicial Magistrate, Chidawa, vide order
dated 14.06.2017, found the petitioner-accused guilty for the
offence under Section 138 of the NI Act and sentenced him to
undergo simple imprisonment for 2 (two) years. The petitioner-
accused was also directed to pay an amount of Rs. 30,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty Lakhs), as compensation under Section 357(3) of
the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, (for short ‘the Code’).
7. The petitioner-accused challenged the said order dated
14.06.2017  before the  Additional Sessions  Judge, Chidawa,
Dist. Jhunjhunu, by filing Criminal Appeal No. 39/2017 which
was dismissed on 10.04.2019.
8. The  petitioner-accused  challenged  the  order  dated
10.04.2019, passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Chidawa,
before the High Court, by filing a S.B. Criminal Revision
Petition being No. 1097 of 2019. The High Court, vide order

--- Page 84 ---
4
dated 18.02.2020, directed the petitioner-accused to surrender
before the Trial Court and furnish bail bonds accordingly. In
compliance of the order dated 18.02.2020, the petitioner-
accused surrendered before the Trial Court on 25.02.2020 and
furnished bail bonds.
9. The respondent filed an application (IA No. 1/2020) under
Section  482  of  the  Code  for  recall  of  the  order  dated
18.02.2020.
10. After hearing the counsel for the petitioner-accused, the
High  Court,  on  13.08.2024,  recalled  the  order  dated
18.02.2020, on noticing that the petitioner-accused was not
present  in  the  court  on  one  occasion,  has  directed  the
petitioner to surrender and cancelled the bail bonds.
11. Ld. Single Judge of the High Court, vide order dated
08.04.2025, dismissed the revision petition holding that the
petitioner has failed to surrender for not complying with the
directions, on multiple occasions, and also in violation of
Rules 311 and 323 of the Rajasthan High Court Rules and also
contrary to Section 389 of the Code.
12. Aggrieved, the petitioner-accused has filed the present
special leave petitions challenging the orders of the High
Court  dated  13.08.2024  and  08.04.2025  in  S.B.  Criminal
Revision Petition No.1097 of 2019.
13. Heard  Ms.  Vandana  Sehgal,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner and Mr. Puran Mal Saini, learned counsel for the
respondent.
14. When  SLP  (Crl.)   No(s).   7001/2026  @  Diary  No(s).

--- Page 85 ---
5
17233/2026  came  up  for  hearing  before  this  Court  on
15.04.2026, the following order was passed:-
“1. Applications for exemption from filing certified
copy of  the impugned  judgment and  exemption from
filing official translation are allowed.

against the order dismissing the Revision Petition
also a Special Leave Petition has been filed under
Diary No.17208 of 2026.
5. Insofar  as the  present petition  is concerned,
learned counsel draws attention of the Court to page
79 of the paperbook (pdf 94) wherein pending the
Revision Petition, the High Court by order dated 18th
February, 2020 permitted the petitioner to surrender
before the Trial Court and furnish bail bonds as
directed in the order. Learned counsel further draws
attention to page 80 (pdf 95) of the paperbook to

25th February, 2020 and the petitioner was on bail

that is a challenge (revision petition) to the consequential

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
Criminal Appeal No.109 of 2017 
 
 
Om Pal & Ors.      ...Appellants 
 
 
Versus 
 
The State of Uttarakhand & Anr.        ...Respondents 
 
O R D E R 
 
 The order dated 24.08.2026 in the above matter is 
recalled. 
2. Having heard Sri Yashraj Singh Deora, learned Senior 
Counsel appearing for the appellant s and the Government 
Advocate as also perusing the records, we are not satisfied 
that there is any valid ground for interference  being caused 
to the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and the High 
Court, especially under Article 136 of the Constitution. 
However, we notice that the first appellant is entitled  to 
remission for which he could make an application to the 
Government, which shall be considered based on the policy 
at the time of the incident or any other beneficial policy , 
subsequently brought in, as applicable to the said accused. 

--- Page 96 ---
Page 2 of 4 
 
 
3. We are informed that  the first and the third 
appellant/accused have served more than 11 years in 
custody, and the second appellant /accused is no more.   
Hence, we direct that the first accused be released on such 
terms and conditions imposed by the Trial Court, forthwith 
subject to the consideration of his application for remission. 
4. The accused , on release , shall be assisted by the 
District Legal Services Authority  (DLSA) to make an 
application for remission; if he desires so. 
5. The second accused is no more and his appeal stands 
abated. 
6. Insofar as the third appellant is concerned, he has not 
completed the period required for consideration of 
remission.  
7. We take notice of the Uttarakhand Jail Manual, 2023, 
more particularly Clause 522 which speaks of consideration 
of eligibility for sentence pardon/ premature release . We 
extract herewith sub clause (iii) of Clause 522 which is as 
under: - 
“All convicted prisoners to life imprisonment whose have 
completed the age of 70 years or above of age, and have 

--- Page 97 ---
Page 3 of 4 
 
 
completed the sentence of 10 years without remission and 
12 years with remission including the under-trial period.” 
 
8. The first appellant who is 80 years old falls  squarely 
under the above provision.  Hence, we direct  that on his 
attaining the period for consideration of remission, his case 
shall be considered by the State Government under  that 
policy, so as to release him on remission. The Superintendent 
of the Jail shall ensure that on completion of remission, the 
third appellant is given due assistance through DLSA to make 
an application for remission before the appropriate authority 
in the State Government. 
9. The third appellant is on bail and he shall hence 
surrender within a period of three weeks from today.  
10. The Registry of this Court shall forward a copy of this 
order to the Member Secretary, Uttarakhand State Legal 
Services Authority, who shall coordinate with the concerned 
DLSA and ensure due compliance of the directions issued by 
this Court. 
11. Appeal though rejected, the directions above shall be 
complied with.

Page 4 of 4 
 
 
 
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

         IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.             /2026
[Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.14415/2026]
SANKET TAILOR                           APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN                     RESPONDENT
WITH
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.             /2026
[Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.14664/2026]
PRATEEK CHAUDHARY      APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN                     RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at
1

--- Page 110 ---
Jaipur has declined the prayers of the appellants, Sanket
Tailor and Prateek Chaudhary, for grant of bail. Their
applications1 stand dismissed by separate judgments and
orders dated 30th June, 2026.
3. These appeals take exception to such dismissal.
4. Both the appellants figure as accused in FIR No.0008 of
2026 dated 04 th February, 2026 registered at Police Station
Special Police Station-SOG, District ATS & SOG, Rajasthan
under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 & 120-B of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 and Section 66D of the Information
Technology (Amendment) Act, 2008. While Sanket Tailor was
arrested on 26 th March, 2026, Prateek Chaudhary  was
arrested on 25th March, 2026.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the counter-affidavit of the respondent-State of
Rajasthan.
6. It  is  not  in  dispute  that  upon  completion  of
investigation, chargesheet 2 qua Sanket Tailor and Prateek
1 S. B. Criminal Miscellaneous Bail Application Nos.8678/2026 and 
5902/2026 respectively. 
2 Chargesheet No.10A/2026
2

--- Page 111 ---
Chaudhary has been filed on 19 th June, 2026. Prosecution
proposes to record the evidence of 55 (fifty five) witnesses to
drive home the charges against the appellants. However, the
charges have not been framed and 18th September, 2026 is
the next date fixed before the trial court for framing of
charges. Thus, the trial is likely to take some time to
conclude. 
7. Appellants have been behind bars for quite some time.
They have no criminal antecedents.
8. Also, six co-accused have been enlarged on bail by the
High Court; the appellants are, thus, entitled to claim parity.
9. Taking an overall view of the matter, we are of the
considered opinion that further detention of the appellants’
pending trial is not necessary; and, since the appeals
deserve acceptance, the appellants may be admitted to an
order for grant of bail.
10. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgments and
orders.
11. Appellants  shall  be  released  on  bail,  subject  to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court
3

--- Page 112 ---
and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be
imposed by it.
12. Needless to observe, if released on bail, the appellants
shall not, directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of
the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
13. In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty
to cancel the bail of the appellants.
14. It is also ordered that the appellants shall diligently
attend proceedings of the trial, unless exempted. If they
abstain from attending the proceedings without justifiable
cause, that could also be seen as breach of the conditions for
grant of bail and the trial court will be free to pass
appropriate orders.
15. We clarify that the observations made in this order and
grant of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of
the case.
16. The appeals are, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid
terms.
4

--- Page 113 ---
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Heard Ms. Pragati Neekhra, learned counsel for the

Advocate General (AAG) for the respondent-State of

2. Leave granted.
3. These appeals have been filed against the order
1

--- Page 123 ---
dated 05.04.2023 passed by the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh at Jabalpur in Criminal Appeal No.6 of 1995, by
which, the  conviction and  sentence awarded  to the
appellants has been upheld.
4. During the course of proceedings, learned counsel
for the appellants took a stand that even otherwise,
this Court may consider the fact that the appellants
are in actual custody for more than 15 years, and thus
deserve to be given the benefit of remission for the
entire period, which would entitle them for premature
release. It was submitted that the controversy in the
present case relates to the period which they had spent
prior to conviction, which was almost six years. Thus,
according to learned counsel for the appellants, it
would be violative of their rights under Article 21 of
the  Constitution  of  India,  as  also  against  the
principles of natural justice if a person has to suffer
for an event/situation in which he had absolutely no
role. In support of the contention that such pre-
conviction period spend in custody has also to be
counted for grant of remission, learned counsel relied
upon the Constitution Bench judgment of this Court in
2

--- Page 124 ---
the case of Bhagirath & Ors. vs. Delhi Administration1.
5. Learned AAG for the respondent-State of Madhya
Pradesh  fairly  submits  that  in  view  of  the  said
judgment, the Court may pass appropriate orders.
6. Having considered the matter, we find that since
the actual period of incarceration of the appellants is
over 15 years, and as we are informed by learned
counsel for the appellants that there is no other case
filed against them for any misconduct during the period
of  incarceration,  we  find  that  a  case  for  their
premature release is made out.
7. Accordingly, the Competent Authority is directed
to consider the case of the appellants for premature
release by counting the entire period of incarceration,
including the pre-conviction period for the purposes of
computation  of  remission  and  pass  appropriate
consequential orders.  The same  be done  within two
weeks’ from today.
8. The  appeals  stand  disposed  of  in  the
aforementioned terms.
9. Learned AAG for the respondent-State of Madhya
Pradesh shall communicate the order immediately to the

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard learned Senior Counsels appearing for the parties in extenso. 
2. By  the  impugned  judgment  dated  02.05.2025  rendered  in  W.P.
No.10150/2024  and  W.P.  No.15559/2024,  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  of
Bombay has upheld the order of the Tribunal and dismissed the writ Petitions.
Upon  perusal  of  the  impugned  judgment,  it  would  emerge  therefrom  that
finding recorded by the Tribunal with reference to Clause 5 of the GR dated
04.05.2023, which was questioned, has been held to be unconstitutional by the
Tribunal  to  the  extent  it  restricted  its  applicability.  The  benefit  of  the  GR
dispensing with the Non-Creamy Layer Certificate was made applicable to all
recruitment  that  commenced  from  17.09.2021  (when  advertisement
No.83/2021 was issued). This has been found to be irrational, namely, Clause 5
as  it  created  sub-clause  within  female  candidates  by  excluding  those
recruitment  which  had  commenced  after  advertisement  No.83/2021  but
concluded before 29.09.2022, as being without any rational basis or intelligible
differentia. This finding of the Tribunal, which was sought to be set aside by the
2

--- Page 142 ---
writ  petitioner  before  the  High  Court,  has  been  succinctly  discussed  in
threadbare,  and  negatived  the  said  contentions  by  the  High  Court  vide
paragraph Nos.14, 15, 17 and 19 and for ready reference, we extract the same
as under:
“14. The Tribunal while considering the challenge to Clause 5 of
the GR dated 04/05/2023 found that the said Clause created three sub-
classes  from  the  broader  class  of  females.  The  first  sub-class  was
female  candidates  who  had  participated  in  the  recruitment  process
pursuant to Advertisement No. 83 of 2021. The second sub-class was of
female candidates, who had participated in the recruitment process that
commenced after publication of Advertisement No. 83 of 2021 but the
results of such recruitment were declared prior to 29/09/2022. The third
sub-class created was of female candidates who had participated in the
recruitment process which commenced after 29/09/2022. The benefit of
Clause 5 was extended to the first and third sub-classes while such
benefit was not granted to candidates in sub-class two. The Applicants
fall in sub-class two. The Tribunal found that there was no rationale in
creating such sub-classes within a common class and that Clause 5 of
the GR dated 04/05/2023 was discriminatory in nature. On that basis,
the Tribunal proceeded to hold that Clause 5 of the said GR to the
extent its restricted its applicability limited to Advertisement No. 83 of
2021 and the recruitment process that commenced after 29/09/2022
was unconstitutional. Benefit of Clause 5 was made applicable to all
recruitment that commenced from 17/09/2021 when Advertisement No.
83 of 2021 was issued.
15. Perusal of the GR dated 04/05/2023 indicates that the decision to
do away with the submission of Non-Creamy Layer Certificate by women
candidates seeking appointment from the open category as well as from
the reserved category has been done away with. This decision though
taken on 04/05/2023, has been made specifically applicable only to
Advertisement No. 83 of 2021 and to advertisements published after
completion of the recruitment process under Advertisement No. 83 of
2021. This process was completed on 29/09/2022. In effect therefore,
the  GR  has  a  retrospective  operation  from  the  publication  of
Advertisement  No.  83  of  2021  on  17/09/2021  and  thereafter  from
29/09/2022  onwards.  There  does  not  appear  any  justification
whatsoever for excluding the application of this GR to advertisements
issued alongwith or shortly after the Advertisement No. 83 of 2021 was
published.
While there is no challenge to the retrospective applicability of this
GR,  the  issue  pertains  to  excluding  advertisements  issued  after
17/09/2021 and where the recruitment process was completed prior to
29/09/2022. It was incumbent upon the Department of  Women and
Child Welfare to have placed on record some material to indicate as to
why such distinction in the applicability of the said GR was made. In the
matter of choice of a cut-off date, it is well settled that such choice is
within the domain of the executive authority and that the choice of a
cut-off date should not be interfered with unless the decision appears to
be blatantly discriminatory or arbitrary. It is only if a violation of Article
14 of the Constitution of India is found that there would be a scope for
interference. If it is found that a cut-off date has been arbitrarily fixed or
3

--- Page 143 ---
that it has been fixed without any rational basis whatsoever, the same
could be a reason for interference. At the same time, merely on the
ground  that  certain  degree  of  arbitrariness  may  appear  to  have
resulted,  the  same  by  itself  cannot  be  the  basis  for  the  Court  to
interfere. Even if no particular reason is given for the choice of a cut-off
date, such choice cannot be held to be arbitrary unless it is shown to be
totally capricious or whimsical. 
17. Another aspect on which there was considerable debate was the
aspect of changing “the rules of the game” after it had commenced. It
was urged that the Applicants were bound by the terms and conditions
stipulated  in  Advertisement  No.  12  of  2022  and  therefore  on  the
commencement  of  said  recruitment  process  on  14/02/2022,  the
requirement of submitting a Non-Creamy Layer Certificate could not
have been dispensed with. It is well settled that the selection process
has  to  be  conducted  strictly  in  accordance  with  the  terms  and
conditions stated in the advertisement unless the power of relaxation of
any  terms  and  conditions  is  specifically  reserved.  The  Constitution
Bench in case of Tej Prakash Pathak and others (supra)  has held that
the eligibility criteria that has been notified at the commencement of
the  recruitment  process  cannot  be  changed  midway  through  the
recruitment  process  unless  the  concerned  rules  so  permit  or  if
permissible under the advertisement. Even if the change is permissible,
such change would have to meet the requirement of Article 14 of the
Constitution of India and satisfy the test of non-arbitrariness.
19. Coming to the finding recorded by the Tribunal that Clause 5 of the
GR dated 04/05/2023 was unconstitutional being violative of Article 16
of the Constitution of India, it can be seen that the GR does create sub-
classes in one class without any rationale behind it. There is also no
nexus of dispensing with furnishing of a Non-Creamy Layer Certificate
by  candidates  who  had  responded  to  Advertisement No.83  of  2021
while  not  granting  similar  latitude  to  candidates  under  subsequent
advertisements issued up to 22/09/2022. In this regard, useful reference
can be made to the decision of the Constitution Bench in Davinder Singh
and others (supra). It has been observed as under:-
“85. The Constitution permits valid classification if two conditions
are fulfilled. First, there must be an intelligible differentia which
distinguishes persons grouped together from others left out of the
group.  The  phrase  "intelligible  differentia"  means  difference
capable of being understood. The difference is capable of being
understood  when  there  is a yardstick  to differentiate  the  class
included and others excluded from the group. In the absence of the
yardstick, the differentiation would be without a basis and hence,
unreasonable. The basis of classification must be deducible from
the provisions of the statute; surrounding circumstances or matters
of common knowledge. In making the classification, the State is
free to recognise degrees of harm. Though the classification need
not be mathematical in precision, there must be some difference
between the persons grouped and the persons left out, and the
difference  must  be  real  and  pertinent.  The  classification  is
unreasonable  if  there  is  "little  or  no  difference".  Second,  the
differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be
achieved by the law, that is, the basis of classification must have a
nexus with the object of the classification. 
93. The test that the Court must follow to determine the
validity of the sub-classification of a class is as follows:
4

--- Page 144 ---
(a)  Whether  the  class  is  “homogeneous”  or  “similarly
situated” for the purpose of the specific law; 
(b) If the answer to (a) above is in the affirmative, the
class cannot be sub-classified; 
(c) If the answer to (a) above is in the negative, the class
can be sub-classified upon the fulfilment of the following
standard:
(i)  There  must  be  a  yardstick  (or  intelligible
differentia) further classifying the class; and
(ii) The yardstick  must have a rational  nexus
with the object of the statute.”
3. The aforestated exclusion was  held to be deemed discriminatory  and
violative  of  Article  16  of  the Constitution  of  India,  as  there  was  no  nexus
between the classification and object of the GR dated 04.05.2023 would be
defeated.
4. In fact, one another argument which was raised consistently before all the
Forums including before this Court was with regard to “rules of the game”
having been changed. Howsoever, attractive the said argument be, we are not
inclined to accept the same for the simple reason that State itself through the
GR has already dispensed with the Non-Creamy Layer certificate requirement
retrospectively for certain recruitment processes. Denying the benefit flowing
therefrom to a similarly situated group would automatically be arbitrary as such
it cannot be accepted.
5. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner has made yet another
valiant attempt to save the situation of behalf of the petitioner by contending
that  this  court  may  exercise  the  power  vested  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution of India to protect the petitioner who has been working pursuant to
the interim orders of this Court. Though the petitioner has worked on the post of
Deputy Director  by way of an interim order, yet the fact remains, a more
5

--- Page 145 ---
meritorious  person,  namely,  respondent  No.4  being  of  the  same  category
cannot be deprived of that post on the ground of she having further tenure left
and  the  decision  of  this  Court  rendered  in  Govardhan  Vs.  State  of
Maharashtra  &  Ors.1 by the Co-ordinate Bench disposed of on 11.11.2025
would not come to the rescue of the petitioner inasmuch as in paragraph No.5
of the said order, it has been clearly held:
“5. Thus, taking note of the peculiar facts of the case , while allowing
the appeal by permitting the appellant to complete the remaining period of
one and a half years of his service, the private respondent shall be given
employment to the post of Talathi thereafter. The needful shall be done
within a period of four weeks from the date  of superannuation  of the
appellant.” 
     (Emphasis supplied by us)
6. For  the  aforestated  reasons,  we  are  not  inclined  to  entertain  these
petitions. Hence, Special Leave Petitions stand dismissed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

ORDER
We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Petitioner is aggrieved by order dated 10.06.2025
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras (briefly
‘the  High  Court’  hereinafter)  rejecting  the  petition
filed by the petitioner for quashing of proceedings in
Crime  No.  719  of  2024  on  the  file  of  the  first
respondent.
3. As per the first information lodged by the defacto
complainant i.e. respondent No. 2, petitioner and others
on the instructions of one Sambo Senthil had threatened
respondent No. 2 and had asked for ‘protection money’. It
is  stated  that  second  respondent  is  a  supplier  and
contractor supplying various machineries for construction
of roads, demolition of structures etc. Petitioner and
other accused persons sought for ‘protection money’ on
the  ground  that  respondent  No.  2  was  carrying  out
contract works in their area. Respondent No. 2 stated
1

--- Page 159 ---
that though the incident happened in the first part of
January, 2023, out of fear he did not report it to the
police. On the basis of the aforesaid first information,
Crime No. 719/2024 was registered at New Washermenpet
Police Station under Sections 294(b), 386 and 506 (2) of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).
4. On 04.08.2025, this Court had issued notice. On
10.08.2026,  on  a  submission  made  on  behalf  of  the
petitioner as well as on behalf of respondent No. 2 that
the parties have arrived at a settlement and seek closure
of proceedings, the following order came to be passed:
“1. Mr. Gopal Sankaranarayanan, learned Senior
counsel for the petitioner has submitted that
Respondent No.2- informant has filed affidavit
stating that the alleged offence is an outcome
of  miscommunication  and  therefore,  seeks
closure of criminal proceedings.2. In view of
the aforesaid statement, list the matter again
on 08.09.2026.3. In the meanwhile, we stay
further proceedings in FIR No.719/2024.”
5. Today, we have read the affidavit filed on behalf of
the  respondent  No.  2,  de-facto  complainant.  In  the
affidavit, he has stated that he did not lodge the first
information out of his free will and volition. The same
was filed under duress. Inspector Mohammed Buhari had
exerted  undue  pressure  upon  him  to  implicate  the
petitioner whereafter he lodged the first information.
6. While learned counsel for the petitioner and the
2

--- Page 160 ---
second respondent requested the court to exercise its
powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India and
to quash the proceedings, learned state counsel, on the
other  hand,  vehemently  objected  to  the  same.  His
contention is that a  prima facie  offence is made out
against  the  petitioner  which  is  non-compoundable.  He
submits  that  investigation  is  complete,  whereafter
chargesheet has been filed. At this stage, question of
quashing of proceedings would not arise.
7. We  have  given  our  anxious  consideration  to  the
submissions made.
8. While rejecting the petition of the petitioner, the
High Court has held as follows:
“5. On reading of the allegations made in the
complaint and the First Information Report,
this Court finds that there are prima facie
allegations to proceed further. Once the Court
finds that there exist prima facie allegations,
it is for the Investigating Officer to conduct
investigation and lay charge sheet. This Court
cannot conduct roving enquiry in the petition
under Section 528 BNSS at this stage. The
Hon’ble Apex Court time and again held that
exercising power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and
528 BNSS should not be automatic and it should
be exercised sparingly. In the present case,
the reasons and grounds taken by the petitioner
are not enough to quash the FIR at this stage.
Therefore, this Court is not inclined to grant
the prayer sought for by the petitioner.”
9. We have carefully perused the contents of the FIR as
3

--- Page 161 ---
well  as  of  the  affidavit  filed  on  behalf  of  the
respondent No. 2. We are unable to persuade ourselves to
agree with the submissions made on behalf of the second
respondent  that  he  had  lodged  the  first  information
against the petitioner, not out of his free volition but
under duress. We do not think the present case to be a
fit one for quashing of criminal proceedings. It is not a
case  where  we  should  invoke  our  jurisdiction  under
Article  142  of  the  Constitution  of  India.  In  the
circumstances, we decline to interfere with the impugned
order passed by the High Court and dismiss the Special
Leave Petition.
10. Notwithstanding  dismissal  of  the  Special  Leave
Petition, it would be open to the petitioner to seek his
remedy in accordance with law before the trial court.
11. All contentions are kept open.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

1

--- Page 165 ---
Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The petitioners are aggrieved with the impugned judgment
which directed initiation of action on the petition filed by
the 4th respondent under Section 7-A of the U.P. (Regulation of
Building Operations) Act, 19581. 
2. It is submitted that the said direction would run counter
to the consent, as expressed by the 4 th respondent in an order
dated 21.02.2024, produced as Annexure P9, in Writ-C No.1726
of 2024, wherein proceedings were directed to be taken under
Section 10 of the RBO Act. 
3. On facts, suffice it to notice that the parties have
adjacent properties. The 1st petitioner having obtained a lease
and his wife, the 2 nd petitioner, by a sale from the original
owner  of  adjacent  properties.  Adjacent  to  it,  the  4 th
respondent also purchased an extent of property in the very
same Gata No.796 from the original landowner. The petitioners
submitted building plans which were sanctioned on 20.01.2005
and 18.05.2022 while construction was going on as per the
latest sanction, the 4 th respondent approached the Prescribed
Authority, the 2 nd respondent, who issued a notice under
Section 10 of the RBO Act and by an interim order, stayed the
construction.
4. The  petitioners  filed  a  writ  petition  specifically
seeking for initiation of a proceeding under Section 7-A of
1 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the RBO Act’
2

--- Page 166 ---
the RBO Act, which was disposed of by Annexure P9, directing
the Prescribed Authority to conclude the proceedings initiated
by issuance of notice under Section 10, expeditiously in
accordance with law. By the impugned order, the High Court
directed to conclude the proceedings instituted against the
opposite party No.4 under Section 7-A of the RBO Act as also
under Section 10 of the RBO Act expeditiously.
5. We have to notice the distinction between Section 7-A and
Section 10 of the RBO Act, both of which have been extracted
in the impugned order. Section 7-A speaks of cancellation of
permission  obtained  under  fraud  or  misrepresentation,  by
which, if the Prescribed Authority is satisfied that the
permission/sanction was granted in consequence of any material
misrepresentation  made  or  any  fraudulent  statement  or
information  furnished,  the  very  permission/sanction  shall
stand cancelled and any work done in accordance with that
permission/sanction, demolished. Section 10 deals with the
erection, re-erection or material change in any building
commenced or carried on or completed in contravention of any
regulation under this Act or without a permission under
Section 6 or in contravention of such permission issued, the
consequence  is  identical  being  the  demolition  of  the
unauthorized construction. 
6. The petitioners’ contention seems to be that, in the
event of a finding of unauthorized construction, there is
3

--- Page 167 ---
regularization possible, whereas if proceedings are taken
under Section 7-A and the permission is cancelled, then the
entire construction would have to be demolished.
7. We notice that the ground taken by the petitioner is two-
fold, that a misrepresentation was made with respect to the
boundaries of the properties and in any event, the minimum
prescribed  setbacks  were  not  available  in  the  proposed
building plans and the building plans were sanctioned in
violation of the provisions of the building byelaws. What
comes forth is both an allegation under Section 7-A and under
Section 10; of misrepresentation and violation of building
laws.
8. According to us, the High Court erred in Annexure P9 in
directing the conclusion of the proceedings under Section 10,
since the specific prayer made by the petitioner therein, the
4th respondent, was for initiation of proceedings under Section
7-A. We are of the opinion that such direction issued would
preempt the consideration by the Prescribed Authority; whose
satisfaction  is  material  at  the  time  of  initiation  of
proceedings. The parties cannot by themselves decide on the
provision under which proceedings are to be taken, which is in
the exclusive domain of the Prescribed Authority, at least at
the first instance.
9. We are of the opinion that the direction in the impugned
order has to be read as a direction to the Prescribed
4

--- Page 168 ---
Authority to decide on whether the proceedings have to be
initiated under Section 7-A or under Section 10 or even under
both the above provisions, looking at the allegations and then
hearing the parties as also conducting an inspection, if it is
found necessary.
10. We, hence, direct the Prescribed Authority to consider
the  issue  as  to  initiation  of  proceedings  either  under
Sections  7-A/10  of  the  RBO  Act  or  under  both,  on  a
consideration of the complaint raised before it. Needless to
say that the petitioners herein shall be entitled to take all
defenses before the Prescribed Authority. 
11. We make it clear that the observations in Annexure P9 or
the impugned judgment shall not govern the initiation of
proceedings by the Prescribed Authority, which shall be on
such authority’s satisfaction as is indicated in the statutory
provision. We too have not touched on the merits of the
matter.
12. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.
(HARPREET KAUR)                               (POOJA SHARMA)
COURT MASTER (SH)                           COURT MASTER (NSH)

1. Leave granted. 
2. The present appeal arises out of  the final order and
judgment dated 10.04.2026 passed by the  High Court of Jharkhand
at Ranchi in Cr.M.P. No. 417 of 2025, whereby the High Court
allowed the cancellation application preferred by Respondent No.
2 (Informant) and cancelled the anticipatory bail previously
granted to the appellant vide order dated 10.10.2023 in A.B.A.
No. 7861 of 2023 in connection with Bariatu P.S. Case No. 52 of
2022 (G.R. Case No. 2515 of 2022) registered for offences under
Sections 498A, 323, 504, 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and
Sections 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act.
3. Heard learned counsel appearing for the appellant, learned
counsel appearing for Respondent No. 1 (State of Jharkhand), and
learned counsel appearing for Respondent No. 2 (Informant).
4. The High Court of Jharkhand initially granted pre-arrest
bail to the appellant on 10.10.2023 in A.B.A. No. 7861 of 2023,
subject to conditions, including an undertaking/condition that
the appellant would keep and maintain Respondent No. 2 with full

--- Page 170 ---
honour and dignity as his lawful wife as and when she resumed
conjugal life.
5. The High Court, vide the impugned order dated 10.04.2026,
cancelled the pre-arrest bail solely on the ground that the
appellant refused to abide by the condition of resuming conjugal
life with Respondent No. 2, treating the same as a breach of his
undertaking given at the time of furnishing bail bonds.
6. Upon perusal of the records, the investigation in Bariatu
P.S. Case No. 52 of 2022 is complete, and the Charge-Sheet (No.
205/2022 dated 31.07.2022) stands filed before the competent
court. The custodial interrogation of the appellant is no longer
required. In view of the above, the impugned judgment and order
dated 10.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Jharkhand in
Cr.M.P. No. 417 of 2025 is hereby set aside.
7. The pre-arrest bail granted to the appellant vide order
dated 10.10.2023 in A.B.A. No. 7861 of 2023 is restored. In the
event of arrest or surrender in connection with Bariatu P.S.
Case No. 52 of 2022 (G.R. Case No. 2515 of 2022), the appellant
(Md.  Tanbir  Raza  @  Tanvir  Raza)  he  shall  be  released  on
anticipatory bail, subject to the conditions the I.O may deem
fit to impose, on condition also of continued cooperation in the
investigation.
8. Once the appellant is released on bail by the I.O, on
directions  issued  by  the  I.O.  or  summons  issued  by  the
jurisdictional court, the appellant shall appear before the
jurisdictional court and furnish bail bonds and ensure due
appearance in the trial.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
   CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
   (Arising out of SLP(Crl.) No.18454 of 2025)
    
HALKAI @PYARELAL                                   APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH                            RESPONDENT
O R D E R
Heard Ms. Iram Majid, learned counsel for the appellant and
Mr. Sridhar Potaraju, learned Additional Advocate General for the
respondent-State of Madhya Pradesh.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of the impugned judgment dated
05.12.2024 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
in Criminal Appeal No.2493 of 2010 by which, the High Court has
upheld the conviction of the appellant as awarded by the III rd
Additional Sessions Judge, Sagar, Madhya Pradesh  vide  judgment
dated 25.10.2010 in Sessions Case No.390 of 2010 under Sections
376-2(f) and 506-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, the
“IPC”) and also the sentence to undergo life imprisonment under
Section 376-2(f) of the IPC along with a fine of Rs.10,000/-
(Rupees Ten Thousand) and in default of payment of fine, rigorous
imprisonment of another six months and under Section 506-B of the

--- Page 185 ---
2
IPC and further to undergo rigorous imprisonment of one year along
with a fine of Rs.500/- (Rupees Five Hundred) and in default of
payment of fine, rigorous imprisonment of another one month.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that there are many
discrepancies in the testimonies of the witnesses which entitles
the appellant to be acquitted at least on the basis of giving him
benefit of doubt. However, it was contended that the Court may, for
the ends of justice, fix the sentence of the appellant instead of
life imprisonment which under normal circumstances, would mean that
the appellant has to be in jail till the end of his natural life.
Learned counsel for the appellant has also assisted the Court with
the facts of the case and the materials on record.
5. Learned Additional Advocate General for the respondent-State
of Madhya Pradesh submits that the crime for which the appellant
had been convicted is heinous in nature and he will be a threat to
the society after coming out of the jail and the Court if inclined,
may impose conditions so that he does not repeat the offence.
6. Having considered the matter in its entirety and going through
the materials on record, this Court is of the view that the
impugned judgment calls for no interference on merits. However, we
are of the considered opinion that the ends of justice would be
served, if the punishment is modified from life imprisonment to
that of twenty years of actual incarceration without remission. 
7. Accordingly, the conviction of the appellant as awarded by the
by the III rd Additional Sessions Judge, Sagar, Madhya Pradesh vide
its judgment dated 25.10.2010 in Sessions Case No.390 of 2010 under
Sections 376-2(f) and 506-B of the IPC and upheld by the High Court

--- Page 186 ---
3
vide  its  impugned judgment dated 05.12.2024 in Criminal Appeal
No.2493 of 2010, is modified to that of twenty years of actual
incarceration without remission.
8. The appeal stands disposed of in the aforementioned terms.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
1

--- Page 195 ---
2. Petitioner has been convicted under Section 302
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) by
the Additional Sessions Judge, Jharsuguda, Odisha in
S.T. Case No.37/43/97 of 2010-13 and sentenced to
undergo Imprisonment for Life and to pay Rs.10,000/-
as fine with a default stipulation.
3. Appeal  filed  by  the  petitioner  against  his
conviction and sentence was rejected by the High
Court  of  Odisha  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’
hereinafter),  vide  the  judgment  and  order  dated
05.09.2022.
4. On the basis of custody certificate, it can be
seen that as of now, petitioner has been in jail for
almost 17 years.
5. On  03.08.2026,  we  had  issued  notice  on  the
Special Leave Petition as well as on the prayer for
bail.
6. This Court, in the case of In Re: Policy Strategy
for Grant of Bail [2025 SCC OnLine SC 349],  recorded
the following conclusions:
“21.  We,  therefore,  record  the  following
conclusions:
a) Where  there  is  a  policy  of  the
appropriate Government laying down guidelines
for consideration of the grant of premature
release under Section 432 of the CrPC or
Section 473 of the BNSS, it is the obligation
of the appropriate Government to consider
cases of all convicts for grant of premature
2

--- Page 196 ---
release as and when they become eligible for
consideration in terms of the policy. In such
a case, it is not necessary for the convict
or  his  relatives  to  make  a  specific
application for grant of permanent remission.
When  the  jail  manual  or  any  other
departmental  instruction  issued  by  the
appropriate Government contains such policy
guidelines,  the  aforesaid  direction  will
apply;
b) We  direct  those  States  and  Union
Territories that do not have a policy dealing
with the grant of remission in terms of
Section 432 of the CrPC or Section 473 of the
BNSS to formulate a policy within two months
from today;
c) Appropriate Government has the power to
incorporate suitable conditions in an order
granting permanent remission. Consideration
of various factors, which are mentioned in
paragraph 13 above by way of illustration, is
necessary before finalizing the conditions.
The conditions must aim at ensuring that the
criminal tendencies, if any, of the convict
remain  in  check  and  that  the  convict
rehabilitates himself in the society. The
conditions should not be so oppressive or
stringent that the convict is not able to
take  advantage  of  the  order  granting
permanent remission. The conditions cannot be
vague  and  should  be  capable  of  being
performed;
d) Order granting or refusing the relief of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons. The order containing reasons should
be immediately communicated to the convict
through the office of the concerned prison.
The copies thereof should be forwarded to the
Secretaries of the concerned District Legal
3

--- Page 197 ---
Services Authorities. It is the duty of the
prison authorities to inform the convict that
he has the right to challenge the order of
rejection of the prayer for the grant of
remission.
e) As held in the case of Mafabhai Motibhai
Sagar, an order granting permanent remission
cannot  be  withdrawn  or  cancelled  without
giving an opportunity of being heard to the
convict.  An  order  of  cancellation  of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons;
f) The District Legal Services Authorities
shall endeavour to implement NALSA SOP in its
true letter and spirit.
g) Further,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall also monitor implementation
of conclusion (a) as recorded above. For this
purpose,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall maintain the relevant date
of the convicts and as and when they become
eligible to a consideration for grant of
premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal
Services  Authorities  shall  endeavour  to
create  a  portal  on  which  the  data  as
aforesaid  can  be  uploaded  on  real  time
basis.”
7. In terms of Paragraph 21(g) of the conclusions
extracted  herein  above,  District  Legal  Services
Authorities  have  been  mandated  to  monitor
implementation of conclusion (a). For this purpose,
the  District  Legal  Services  Authorities  shall
maintain the relevant date of the convicts and as and
when they become eligible for a consideration for
4

--- Page 198 ---
grant of premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal Services
Authorities shall endeavour to create a portal on
which the data as aforesaid can be uploaded on real
time basis.
8. We, therefore, direct the appropriate Government,
i.e. State of Odisha, to consider the case for
permanent remission of the petitioner as per the
applicable remission policy.
9. The  District  Legal  Services  Authority  of
Jharduguda shall do the needful so that the remission
papers of the petitioner can be transmitted to the
State Government for necessary consideration.
10. In  view  of  the  long  incarceration  of  the
petitioner, we direct, as an interim measure, that
the petitioner shall be released on bail from custody
on his Personal Bond.
11. Interim bail granted to the petitioner shall not
be taken as a factor against the petitioner while
considering his case for permanent remission.
12. Let the consideration be carried out within 03
months from today.
13. List thereafter on 15.12.2026.

"68. In the upshot: 
(i) Visually impaired candidates are eligible to
participate in selection for the posts under the
judicial service and hence, Rule 6A of the Madhya

to the extent of prescribing additional requirement

an aggregate score of 70% in the first attempt, is
struck  down  insofar  as  it  applies  to  PwD
candidates. The said rule will be applicable to the
PwD  candidates  insofar  as  it  prescribes  the
educational and other qualifications as eligibility
criteria including the minimum aggregate score of
70% (with relaxation as may be determined like in
the case of SC/ST candidates), but without the
requirement of either that it should be in the
first attempt or that they should have three years’
practice. As a sequel, the impugned order dated

consequential notification dated 17.11.2023 issued

entitled to be considered for participating in the
selection process in the light of this decision. 
(iii) The order of the High Court dated 11.01.2024

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (CRL.) NO. 11333 OF 2026)
RAJESH SINGH       ...APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.     ...RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal arises out the impugned order dated
28.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at
Gwalior, whereby the application of accused-respondent No.2
for grant of bail, was allowed. 
3. The case of the prosecution is that the appellant-
Rajesh Singh Bhadoriya s/o Brij Mohan Bhadoriya lodged a
First Information Report being F.I.R. No. 164 of 2025 at
P.S.: Old Cantonment, District: Gwalior for the offences
punishable under Sections 109, 191(2), 191(3), 296, 115(2),
351(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for
short, ‘B.N.S.’), stating categorically that his father has
been shot at by the respondent No.2-Shivam Singh Tomar and
ultimately, succumbed to injuries at the hospital.
1

--- Page 215 ---
4. In the dying declaration dated 29.05.2025, which is
also on record, it has been categorically stated by the
appellant’s father (deceased) that he was shot at by the
respondent No.2 – Shivam Singh Tomar.
5. The High Court has granted bail on the ground that co-
accused has been granted bail.
6. In our considered opinion, as there was a specific
statement  made  in  the  F.I.R.  as  also  in  the  dying
declaration, bail should not have been granted in the
manner and method adopted by the High Court. For reference,
the dying declaration dated 29.05.2026 is reproduced as
under: 
“On being questioned, [he] stated that I live at
home and I have two sons, Rajesh and Rakesh. The
incident is of the night of 21.05.25 around 10-11
PM. I was on the roof of the house, and the sound
of fighting and quarreling came from the door of the
house below. I hurried down and saw that Rajesh,
Rakesh, grandson Abhay, and neighbor Mukesh were
being beaten. They had lathis (sticks), dandas
(batons), and axes in their hands. Among them, I
know  Shivpratap  Kushwah  Rajawat,  Manoj  Kushwah
Rajawat, and Shivam Tomar. Manoj is Shivpratap's
uncle. Manoj told Shivam and Shishupal to "shoot
him," so they fired at me, which hit me on the right
hand and waist. I fell unconscious on the ground.
There were 5-6 people fighting in the crowd, and
people nearby were watching the fight. Currently, my
treatment is going on.
I am admitted. The statement has been read over and
heard. This is my statement, accepted as correct.”
2

--- Page 216 ---
7. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
has also supported the case of the appellant. 
8. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent No.2-
Shivam Singh Tomar has admitted before this Court that in
the F.I.R. as well as in the dying declaration, there is a
specific statement made against the respondent No.2. 
9. In light of the above, this Court is of the opinion
that the impugned order passed by the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh in Misc. Criminal Case No. 19504 of 2026 deserves
to be set aside. Hence, the impugned order passed by the
High Court stands set aside and the respondent No.2 is
directed to surrender before the appropriate authority
within a period of two weeks from today.
10. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in the above
terms. 
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

would  hasten  to  add  that  if  one  year’s  time  is

for the offence punishable under Sections 366 and 376(2)
(i) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short the ‘IPC’)

CRL.A.No.4210/2026
(@ SLP (CRL.) No.13037/2026)

Thousand) under Section 366 of IPC and life imprisonment
till his natural life along with a fine of Rs.10,000/-
(Rupees Ten Thousand) under Section 376(2)(i) of IPC.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
sentence  is  excessively  harsh  as  it  envisages
incarceration till the natural life of the appellant. It
is submitted that the Courts have taken a view that such
sentence  should  not  be  passed  as  a  matter  of
course/routine. It was submitted that in the present
case, though there are points available to him to argue
on merits, but without getting into the same, the Court
may consider that such term of sentence may be reduced to
a fixed period.
5. Learned counsel for the State submitted that the
crime is heinous in nature and even if the term is
reduced  to  life  sentence  simplicitor,  his  case  for
premature release could not be favorably considered as
under the policy of the State, such type of crime is not
covered for such premature release.
6. Having considered the matter in its entirety, we
find that the interest of justice would be served without
interfering in the conviction, if the sentence is reduced
2

--- Page 240 ---
CRL.A.No.4210/2026
(@ SLP (CRL.) No.13037/2026)

excluding remission.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties and particularly, take note of the
arguments  of  Mr.  Shanthkumar  V.  Mahale,  learned
senior counsel appearing for the petitioner that the
cause/complaint pending before the High Court is
confined to the limited scope of working arrangement

--- Page 243 ---
2
or interim arrangement made by the Trial Court in the
order impugned passed in Writ Petition No. 23104 of
2024.
2. In  a  situation  as  the  present,  firstly,
calling for a report from  National Institute of
Mental  Health  and  Neurosciences  (‘ NIMHANS’)  is
unnecessary besides being psychologically straining
and  stressful  to  the  ward.  Further,  the
recommendation of NIMHANS for four weeks inpatient
evaluation will expose the child to serious adverse
circumstances in the hospital. Lastly, it is stated
that the writ petition is listed before the High
Court  on  16.09.2026  and  the  High  Court  can  be
requested to dispose of the Writ Petition No. 23104
of 2024 without subjecting the ward to the ordeal of
inpatient assessment at NIMHANS.
3. Mr. Rakesh Kini, learned counsel appearing for
the respondent argues that the reason for calling a
report from experts is to find out whether the ward
is  speaking  the  parroted sentences,  or  being
subjected to stress and strain to speak the voice of
the father or whether the ward is suffering from any
mental difficulty or disability in the circumstances
which would require medical attention and nothing
more.
4. It is further stated if four weeks evaluation

--- Page 244 ---
3
as an inpatient in NIMHANS is on the higher side
tentatively a brief period spell can be considered
for securing the report from an expert Board which is
useful for proper disposal of the pending application
in Writ Petition No. 23104 of 2024.
5. We take note of the submissions and are of the
view that calling for a report at this stage of the
matter ought to be the last option in a matter as the
present. When we observed so, we do not mean that the
Court does not have power to secure a report on the
condition of the ward but in the circumstances of the
case whether the discretion in that direction is
required to be exercised or not is the point we are
considering.
6. Taking note of the order of the Trial Court
and  the  order  dated  28.04.2026  impugned  in  the
special leave petition, we are of the view that the
High Court can be requested to dispose of the writ
petition on the next date of hearing, if convenient.
7. Both the parties are given liberty to place
before the Court medical evidence in support of their
respective contentions and the High Court by looking
at evidence brought on record by the parties, will
consider whether there is a need to call for report
from an expert body or not. In other words, the High
Court, if decides to dispose of the writ petition on

--- Page 245 ---
4
merits from the available record, the High Court is
requested to dispose of the writ petition. 
8. With the above observations, the special leave
petition is disposed of.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.

and seeks regular bail in connection with FIR

Pradesh for the offence punishable under Section

3. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the appellant and the learned counsel appearing
for the respondent - State.
4. It is pertinent to note that not only has the
co-accused person(s) been granted the benefit of
bail, the fact remains that the appellant has
been  under  incarceration  for  a  period  of
1  SLP(CRL.) No.11959/2026

approximately  11  months  and  the  trial  has

antecedents, in which the appellant is allegedly
said to be involved.

inclined to set aside the impugned order passed
by  the  High  Court,  and  grant  bail  to  the
appellant.

aside, and the appellant is granted regular
bail, subject to the terms and conditions that
may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the appellant and the learned counsel appearing
for the State.
3. The appellant was convicted by the Trial Court
for the offences punishable under Sections 341,
324, 326, 307 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 (for short, the ‘IPC’)  and  sentenced to
undergo simple imprisonment for a period of ten
years. 
4. Aggrieved by the same, the appellant preferred a
criminal  appeal  challenging  his  conviction
before the High Court in the year 2025.  The
appellant  then  filed  an  application  seeking
1 SLP(CRL.) No.10281/2026

--- Page 263 ---
suspension of sentence during the pendency of
his appeal before the High Court, which has been
dismissed vide the impugned order.  Hence, the
present appeal has been filed.
5. Admittedly, the appellant has already completed
actual sentence of more than four years out of
the imposed sentence of 10 years.
6. Taking note of the aforesaid factual scenario
alone, we are inclined to set aside the impugned
order and suspend the sentence of the appellant
till  the  disposal  of  the  criminal  appeal,
pending before the High Court, and grant bail to
the appellant.
7. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands  set
aside, the appellant’s sentence stands suspended
during the pendency of the appeal before the
High Court, and the appellant shall be released
on bail, subject to the terms and conditions to
the satisfaction of the concerned Trial Court,
unless he is required in any other case. 
8. The appeal is allowed, accordingly.
2 SLP(CRL.) No.10281/2026

disposed of.

A W A R D
1. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner/claimant
and the learned counsel for the Insurance Company instructed by
the  Officer(s)/Official(s)  represented  by  the  National
Insurance Company Limited.
2. Considering it is a case of amputation, we put it to the
Insurance Company that applying the judgment of this Court in
Civil Appeal No.4642/2026 titled as “ Prahlad Sahay vs. Haryana
Roadways & Anr. , dated 21.04.2026, reported in 2026 INSC 396,
and the law laid down by therein, the injured claimant is
entitled to the facility of a prosthetic limb till the age of
70.
3. We  also  put  it  to  the  Insurance  Company  that  the
petitioner/claimant was 32 years of age on the date of the
accident and he is entitled upto 7 prosthetic limbs apart from
annual maintenance. The normal cost of a reasonably good
prosthetic limb is Rs.3,00,000/- approximately. The annual
maintenance worked out to Rs. 10,000/- to 15,000/- per annum.
4. We had suggested that the petitioner/claimant would be
entitled to 8 prosthetic limbs. However, the Insurance Company
pointed out that cost of one prosthetic limb has already been
given by the employer.

--- Page 268 ---
3
5. We  suggested  to  the  Insurance  Company  that
petitioner/claimant is entitled to 7 prosthetic limbs along
with maintenance charges.
6. The  Insurance  Company  stated  that  in  this  case  the
consolidated amount will be awarded, on the peculiar facts of
this case.
7. Parties have now agreed that a consolidated amount of
Rs.30,00,000/-, over and above the amount, awarded by the High
Court will be paid to the petitioner/claimant.
8. The  said  consolidated  amount  will  be  paid  by  the
Insurance  Company  within  eight  weeks’  from  today  to  the
petitioner/claimant.
9. On payment of such amount, the petitioner/claimant will
have no further claims against the Insurance Company.
10. Learned counsel for the petitioner/claimant may furnish
the bank account details of the petitioner/claimant to the
learned  counsel  for  the  Insurance  Company.  Subject  to
verification  and  identity,  the  amount  be  paid  to  the
petitioner/claimant, directly.
11. We record our appreciation to the fair stand taken by
learned counsel for the petitioner/claimant and the learned
counsel for the Insurance Company and Mr.Jeet Singh Khurana
representing the Insurance Company, for the positive attitude
displayed by them in bringing an amicable end to the dispute in
this matter.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No. 933 OF 2018
SAHENDRA SINGH ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. This Criminal Appeal takes exception to the judgment and order
dated 03.07.2015 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna
(‘High Court’ hereinafter) in Criminal Appeal (DB) No.431/2008
reversing the conviction of the respondent and acquitting him of
the charges after holding him not guilty.
3. It may be mentioned that vide the judgment and order dated
29.02.2008, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Fast
Track Court No. Vth, Gaya, in Sessions Trial No.14 of 2007 / 39 of
2007, respondent Nitya Nand Sharma was convicted under Sections
148, 302 and 386 read with Sections 120B and 149 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) as well as under Section 27 of the Arms Act,
1959. Following such conviction, the respondent was sentenced to
suffer imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of 10,000/- (Rupees₹
Ten Thousand Only) with a default stipulation for the offence under
Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC; he was sentenced to undergo
Rigorous Imprisonment (RI) for a period of 5 years and to pay a
fine of 3,000/- with a default stipulation for the offence under₹
1

--- Page 279 ---
Section 386 read with Section 120B IPC; for his conviction under
Section 148 IPC, the respondent was sentenced to undergo RI for a
period of 3 years and for his conviction under Section 27 of the
Arms Act, he was also sentenced to undergo RI for a period of 3
years and to pay a fine of 3,000/- with a default stipulation; all₹
the sentences were directed to run concurrently.
4. As stated above, vide the judgment and order dated 03.07.2015,
the High Court set aside the aforesaid conviction and sentence and
acquitted the respondent.
5. The de-facto complainant preferred the related Special Leave
Petition on which notice was issued on 28.09.2015. Thereafter,
leave was granted on 23.07.2018.
6. In the hearing held on 23.07.2026, learned counsel for the
respondent  submitted  that  he  had  received  information  that
appellant had passed away on 20.11.2019. We granted time to learned
counsel for the appellant to obtain instructions from the family of
the de-facto complainant as to whether they would like to pursue
the appeal and if they were inclined to pursue the appeal, liberty
was  granted  to  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  to  file
appropriate  application  to  bring  them  on  record.  Thereafter,
further time was granted to learned counsel for the appellant.
7. Today learned counsel for the appellant submits that though he
got in touch with the family members of the de-facto complainant,
no instructions have been furnished to him whether to pursue the
appeal or not.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent submits that he had already
undergone incarceration for more than nine and a half years before
2

--- Page 280 ---
his acquittal by the High Court.
9. In the circumstances, we are of the view that since if there
is none to pursue the appeal, the same stands abated.
10. Consequently the Criminal Appeal is dismissed as abated.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
......................J.
(UJJAL BHUYAN)
......................J.
(ATUL S. CHANDURKAR)
NEW DELHI;
September 08th, 2026.
